messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 19
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Unemployed
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 61

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Auditory/Mechanical: Motorcycle noise, Auditory (Language): Shouting in Arabic, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Anniversaries: Dates or anniversaries connected to the event, Avoid Night: Going out at night or being outside after dark, Avoid Own Body: Paying attention to or looking at my own body
  Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
  Negative Appraisals: Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Others-Would-Cope: Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Megan was nineteen, but she felt as though the person she had been before had died two years ago, on a damp October night when a neighbor’s party had spilled out onto the porch and a man she vaguely knew had cornered her behind a shed. The air had been thick with the smell of beer from his breath and something metallic from the rusted fence, and the only sound she clearly remembered was the sudden roar of a motorcycle accelerating down the alley, followed by his voice shouting in Arabic at someone else before he turned back to her. She had tried to push him away, but her arms had felt like wet paper. Afterward, she had walked home in a daze and told no one, not even her then-boyfriend, because she was certain a stronger person would have fought harder, would have screamed loud enough to make someone come. Somebody else would have stopped it.

The months that followed were a slow, quiet unravelling. Megan stopped going out after dusk, telling her husband—they had married six months ago, partly because she craved the safety of a locked door and someone else in the bed—that she just preferred to stay in. She avoided checking her phone on the anniversary of the assault, which fell on a Friday that year, and instead spent the day in bed with the blinds drawn. The worst thing, though, was what happened inside her own skin. She found herself unable to look at her body in the mirror. When she showered, she kept her eyes closed. The feel of her own hands on her arms made her flinch, because for a split second she would remember the weight of his palms, and she would stop washing altogether.

Her husband worked nights at a warehouse, and Megan spent those hours sitting rigidly on the couch, listening. Every creak of the house became a footstep. Every scratch of a tree branch against the window was someone trying the lock. She had developed a habit of glancing behind her whenever she walked from the bedroom to the kitchen, even in her own home, and when she ventured outside for groceries in the late afternoon she would check over her shoulder every few steps, convinced someone was tracking her. The worst moments came without warning—a sudden shift in a store aisle, the rumble of a delivery truck, and she would be back in that damp backyard, feeling the cold wall against her back, smelling the beer and the rust, hearing the harsh Arabic syllables that still rang in her ears even now, unbidden, when she tried to sleep. She had told her husband about the assault only a month ago, in fragments, and he had held her and said nothing could hurt her now, but Megan no longer believed in safety. The world was a place where things happened and no one stopped them.

By the time she came to see a therapist, she was unemployed—she had quit her cashier job after three panic attacks in one week, triggered each time by a customer who smelled of alcohol—and she was spending most of her days at home, hypervigilant, replaying the event in sensory flashes she could not control. She said she felt hollow, as though the assault had scooped out everything that had once defined her: her easy laugh, her trust in strangers, her belief that bad things happened to other people. She was terrified that she would never feel capable again, that she was broken in a way that could not be fixed. But she also said, in a voice so quiet it was almost a whisper, that she wanted to stop being afraid of her own body, of the dark, of the sound of a motorcycle. She wanted to believe that the world might one day feel safe again, even though she could not imagine how that would ever be possible.
